title: Moroccan scholarship
hookLine: Fez and Marrakesh as cities of scholars, Sufis and craftsmen

lines: TAP, TAP — A TILE IS CUT.
cards: Tap, tap, tap. In a workshop in Fez, a craftsman holds a small hammer and a square of glazed tile, and chips it into a tiny shape, a star point, a curved petal.
Piece after piece will be laid face down, fitted together like a puzzle and set in plaster, until they become a wall that glitters.

Across the lane, in the courtyard of a college, students sit reading among tiles cut by hands like his. In the old cities of Morocco, the scholar and the craftsman worked within a few steps of each other.

teach.b: In Fez, the city's learning gathered around the mosque of al-Qarawiyyin, founded, as the chronicle you heard last week tells it, by Fatimah al-Fihri.
Around it, rulers and donors added madrasahs: courtyards with a fountain, rooms for students upstairs, a prayer hall, walls of carved cedar, carved plaster and tilework.
Marrakesh, founded by the Almoravids, became another city of learning in the south, with its own mosques, colleges and markets. In both, learning wasn't shut away.
It lived next to the tanneries, the copper beaters and the book binders. Marrakesh also honors a group that tradition calls its seven saints, and the list joins two kinds of learning.
One is Qadi Iyad, a judge and a scholar of hadith and law. Another is al-Jazuli, a Sufi whose book of blessings on the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is still recited.

teach.h: A JUDGE AND A MYSTIC, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: A judge and a mystic, side by side, honored by the same city. And the craftsmen?

teach.h: THE WORK OF YOUR OWN HANDS.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 2072, says nobody has eaten better food than what they earn by the work of their own hands, and that the prophet David ate from the work of his hands.
Work with the hands wasn't a step down from study; it was honored too.
So Moroccan scholarship is wider than a man with a book: the book, the student's room, the cut tile on the wall, the saint's tomb at the end of the lane.

how: In Fez and Marrakesh, historic madrasahs, mosques and saints' tombs are still visited, students still study at al-Qarawiyyin, and crafts such as zellij tilework are still practiced and taught.

games.q: you're a donor in Fez, building a new madrasah for students. you want it to honor learning. what do you do?
o: keep the walls bare so nothing distracts.
fill it with carved cedar, plaster and tilework by the city's craftsmen.
build it outside the city, away from the noise.
games.why: Fez's madrasahs are covered in carved cedar, carved plaster and zellij, the craftsmen's work around the students' study.

practice: Here's a craft word from Morocco: zellij, the cut glazed tilework from the hook; say it quietly.
Then look at your own hands and think of one thing they know how to make or mend, bread, a shelf, a stitch, a careful page of handwriting, and hold that skill in mind the way a scholar holds a text.
If you pray, give thanks for the work of your hands; if you don't, simply notice what they can do.
